1009.title: pranayama sequences
1009.hook: a recipe card says where, how long and how many; one short sutra measures the breath the same way
1009.howItsDone: Some teachers of pranayama shape a sequence with the measures of Yoga Sutra 2.50, adjusting where the breath is felt, how long each part lasts and how many rounds are taken.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pace of a sequence: tame the breath little by little, like a keeper with a lion, gentle first and long holds later.

A grandmother's recipe card, stained at one corner. It barely says anything. Which pot. How long on the flame. How many cardamom pods. Three measures, and somehow the whole dish is in them; change one, and it's a different dish. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras are written like that card. Each line is short enough to memorize, and the explaining is left to the teacher. One line in the second chapter measures the breath, with three measures a cook would recognize.
screen: `A RECIPE CARD.` → `WHICH POT, HOW LONG, HOW MANY.` → `A SUTRA MEASURES THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Sutra two fifty, in paraphrase: pranayama has three movements, the breath going out, the breath coming in, and the breath held still. Each is observed by place, by time and by number, and then the breath becomes long and subtle. Take the measures one at a time. Place, desha: commentators read it as where the breath is felt or reaches, the nostrils, the chest, the belly, or how far out it goes. Time, kala: how long each movement lasts, which is what counting a slow breath measures. Number, sankhya: how many breaths, how many rounds. Here's what that gives a sequence. It can change one measure and keep the other two steady: same place and number, a little more time; or same time, a few more rounds. That's yesterday's slow taming, given handles you can hold. Now the goal the sutra names: not long breaths for their own sake, but long and subtle. The word for subtle, sukshma, means fine, delicate, hard to see. A breath can be long and still rough, like pulling a heavy door. The sutra wants it long and fine, like thread pulled through a needle. So the measures aren't the point. They're how a teacher and a student watch the breath closely enough that it can grow quiet. On this reading, a good sequence is one where the counting slowly matters less, as the breath grows too fine to measure roughly.
screen: `OUT, IN, HELD STILL.` · `PLACE, TIME, NUMBER.` · `CHANGE ONE MEASURE AT A TIME.` · `THE GOAL: LONG AND SUBTLE.`

segments.voice: Find where you feel the breath most right now, the nose, the chest or the belly, and rest there; then count the in-breath and the out-breath, and let them be equal. Choose a small number of rounds, say six, counted on your fingers, and let only the time stretch, one count longer each way. When the rounds are done, let go of all three, and see if the breath is a little finer than when you began.
Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, the three measures a sequence can move: place, time and number, toward a breath long and subtle.
Your line: place, time, number. The goal is a breath long and fine, like thread through a needle. Day one thousand nine.

1010.title: pranayama sequences
1010.hook: an Upanishad sets its breath advice beside pebbles, sand and the sound of water
1010.howItsDone: Some Hindus who keep a daily breath practice begin by choosing a clean, quiet spot and settling the body upright, following the order the Shvetashvatara Upanishad sets out before the breath itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pranayama sequences measured three ways: place, time, number, toward a breath long and subtle.

Level ground. No pebbles. No fire nearby, no sand. Pleasant to the ear, with the sound of water. Out of the wind. It's a checklist a camper would understand, and it sits in one of the Upanishads, right beside its advice on the breath. It sounds almost too practical for a scripture. But place, body, breath and mind all turn up together in a few short verses.
screen: `LEVEL GROUND, NO PEBBLES.` → `OUT OF THE WIND.` → `RIGHT BESIDE THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: The text is the Shvetashvatara Upanishad, chapter two, in paraphrase and in its own order. First the body: hold it steady, chest, neck and head upright, and let the senses, together with the mind, settle into the heart. Then the breath: having restrained the breath, with movements calmed, breathe out gently through the nostrils. Then the mind: hold it the way a charioteer holds a chariot yoked to restless horses. Then, in the next verse, the place: level and clean, free of pebbles, fire and sand, pleasant with the sound of water, easy on the eye, sheltered from the wind. So a sequence isn't only a chain of breathing techniques. It begins before any of them. Where are you sitting? Is the body upright and steady? Only then does the breath have somewhere to settle. Notice the word gently. Not breathe out hard, or hold as long as you can. The strength in this picture belongs to the charioteer's hands, not to the breath. And the horses are restless; the text expects that. It doesn't scold the horses. It asks for a steady driver. The image may be familiar from the Katha Upanishad, where the body is a chariot and the senses are horses; here it turns up in the middle of breath practice. It's close to Patanjali's frame from earlier this week, the seat before the breath, but this Upanishad adds the ground under the seat. So a full sequence, in one reading, runs: place, body, breath, mind. Skip the first two, and the breath is asked to do work the ground and the spine were meant to do.
screen: `THE BODY: CHEST, NECK, HEAD UPRIGHT.` · `THE BREATH: OUT GENTLY, THROUGH THE NOSE.` · `THE MIND: A CHARIOTEER WITH RESTLESS HORSES.` · `THE PLACE: LEVEL, QUIET, OUT OF THE WIND.`

segments.voice: Look at where you are first, and if there's a bag, a cup or a buzzing phone you can move, move it. Let the chest, neck and head stack upright without stiffening, and let each slow out-breath leave gently through the nose. When the mind pulls away like a restless horse, bring it back with a light hand, no scolding.
Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, the frame the Upanishad gives around them: place, body, breath, mind.
Your line: place, body, breath, mind. The text asks for a steady driver, not quiet horses. That's day one thousand ten.

1011.title: pranayama sequences
1011.hook: after all the lengthening and pausing, the Gita's breath lands somewhere plain: even
1011.howItsDone: Some Hindus who practice pranayama close with a few rounds of even breathing, in and out of equal length, a practice teachers connect with Gita 5.27, where the in-breath and out-breath are made even.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pranayama sequences in the Upanishad's order: place, body, breath, mind, with a steady driver for restless horses.

Old brass scales in a spice shop. The shopkeeper drops a weight on one pan and pours cumin into the other, and both pans swing. Then they slow. Then they hang level, the needle pointing straight up. That's the moment the sale is made. Nothing dramatic. Just even. For days now the breath has been offered, tamed, measured and given a place to sit. The Gita, in its fifth chapter, has a line about where breath practice settles, and it's as plain as those scales.
screen: `TWO PANS OF A SCALE.` → `THEY SWING, THEN HANG LEVEL.` → `WHERE DOES THE BREATH SETTLE?`

segments.voice: Bhagavad Gita, chapter five, verses twenty-seven and twenty-eight, in paraphrase: shutting out the outside world, with the gaze resting between the brows, making the in-breath and the out-breath even as they move within the nostrils, with senses, mind and understanding held in check, the sage set on freedom, free of desire, fear and anger, is free indeed. Look at the breath in the middle of that. Not held for a long time. Not forced out. Even: in and out made equal, the two pans hanging level. The Sanskrit word is sama, even, the same. It shows up elsewhere in the Gita too: even in pleasure and pain, even toward friend and foe. Here it reaches all the way down to the breath. And the verse doesn't stop at the nostrils. It goes on to desire, fear and anger falling away. The breath is near the center of the line, but the line is about a person. In this picture, an even breath and an even mind travel together. That gives a sequence a direction. The slow counts, the pauses and the measured rounds can swing the breath one way or another, the way pouring cumin swings the scale. The verse points to where they come to rest: in and out the same, then nothing more to adjust. This block began with the breath the others rise with, then the seat, the offering, the lion, the three measures, the clean ground. It ends here, level. Tomorrow a new block begins: a mantra, kept day after day, laid on that even breath.
screen: `IN-BREATH AND OUT-BREATH MADE EVEN.` · `SAMA: EVEN, THE SAME.` · `AN EVEN BREATH, AN EVEN MIND.` · `WHERE THE SEQUENCE COMES TO REST.`

segments.voice: With place and body settled, let the breath swing a little for a few rounds, a slightly longer out-breath, then a slightly longer in-breath, like the pans moving. Then let them meet, in for four and out for four, quiet within the nostrils, even without strain. When it's steady, stop counting and see if it stays level on its own; if it tips, even it out again, lightly.
Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, where the Gita lets them settle: in-breath and out-breath made even, like scales hanging level.
Your line: the breath made even. In the Gita's picture, an even breath and an even mind travel together. Day one thousand eleven, done.

1012.title: mantra sadhana (a 40-day japa discipline)
1012.hook: Arjuna says holding the mind still is like holding the wind; Krishna doesn't disagree
1012.howItsDone: Hindus who undertake a mantra sadhana may begin with a sankalpa, a resolve naming the mantra, the time, the place and the span, and then keep the practice daily, sometimes with a teacher's guidance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pranayama sequences closed on the Gita's line: the breath made even, like scales hanging level.

The mind is restless, Arjuna says. Turbulent, strong, stubborn. Trying to hold it still, he tells Krishna, seems as hard as holding the wind. It's the sixth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, and Krishna has just described a yogi sitting in perfect steadiness, like a lamp in a windless place. Arjuna's answer is blunt: that sounds lovely, and I can't see how it could last. What's striking is Krishna's reply. He doesn't tell Arjuna he's wrong. He agrees. Then he names the two things that work anyway.
screen: `THE MIND IS LIKE THE WIND.` → `KRISHNA AGREES.` → `THEN HE NAMES WHAT WORKS.`

segments.voice: Gita six, verse thirty-five, in paraphrase: without doubt the mind is restless and hard to hold, but it can be held by practice and by letting go. Practice is abhyasa, steady repeated effort. Letting go is vairagya, loosening the grip of wanting. Hold on to the first: again and again. That's the ground this new block stands on. Its name has two words. Mantra: a sacred sound or phrase, a syllable like Om, a name of God, a line from a text. Sadhana: a practice kept as a discipline, done regularly with a purpose. Together, a mantra returned to on purpose, not said once when the mood is right. The block's title adds japa, repetition, and a span, forty days. Tradition gives spans like that; the verses here don't fix a number, and the coming days look at that. Where does a sadhana begin? In some lineages, with a sankalpa, a resolve said or held at the start. It sets the terms before the effort: which mantra, at what time, where, how long. A sankalpa isn't a mood. It's closer to a promise with the details written in. Here's why that matters, given Arjuna's wind. A restless mind is very good at renegotiating. Later? Shorter today? A different mantra? The sankalpa settles those questions once, at the start, so the mind has less to argue with each morning. Krishna's answer was practice. The sankalpa is how practice gets a shape.
screen: `HELD BY PRACTICE AND LETTING GO.` · `MANTRA: A SACRED SOUND OR PHRASE.` · `SADHANA: A PRACTICE KEPT AS DISCIPLINE.` · `SANKALPA: SET THE TERMS AT THE START.`

segments.voice: Settle the place, the body and a few gentle breaths, the way the pranayama days ended. Without saying any mantra yet, set the terms of a small sadhana: a mantra from your own tradition if you pray, or Om, or a single word that matters to you; a time; a place; and a length small enough to keep. Hold those four clearly, like words on a card, then let them go and sit with the breath.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline, returned to on purpose. It begins with practice, abhyasa, and in some lineages with a sankalpa that sets the terms.
Your line: practice, and a resolve. Krishna agreed the mind is like the wind, and named what holds it anyway. See you tomorrow.

1013.title: mantra sadhana (a 40-day japa discipline)
1013.hook: a string of beads in a coat pocket, one bead larger than the rest, and a rule about never crossing it
1013.howItsDone: Hindus who keep japa may count on a mala, a string of beads of tulsi wood, rudraksha or other materials, moving one bead per repetition and turning the string at the larger meru bead rather than crossing it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mantra sadhana began with Arjuna's wind and Krishna's answer: practice, and a resolve that sets the terms.

In a coat pocket, a loop of beads: small wooden ones, or knobbly dark seeds, worn smooth by a thumb. One bead is larger than the others and sits apart, with a tassel hanging from it. Some who keep japa follow a rule about that big bead. You go all the way round, bead by bead, and when you reach it again you don't step over it. You turn the whole string around and go back the way you came. Why would a bead be something you don't cross?
screen: `A LOOP OF BEADS IN A POCKET.` → `ONE BEAD SITS APART.` → `YOU DON'T CROSS IT.`

segments.voice: The string is called a mala. The word means a garland, like flowers placed around a neck or on an image of God. A japa mala is a garland for counting. The beads vary by tradition. Tulsi wood is tied to devotion to Vishnu and Krishna; rudraksha seeds, the knobbly dark ones, to Shiva. The large bead is the meru, named for the sacred mountain at the center of the world in Hindu cosmology. Teachers in several lineages say not to cross it, and their reasons vary. Some say the meru stands for the guru, or for God, and you don't step over what you honor. Others say turning back keeps the round from becoming mindless, a loop you could spin forever without noticing. Either way, a round has an end, and you know when you've reached it. Now the thread. In the Gita's seventh chapter, Krishna says all of this world is strung on him, like gems on a thread. The beads are what you see; the thread holding them is hidden. Some who keep japa hold that verse in mind as the beads pass: each repetition separate, all strung on one thing. Then the thumb. In the sixth chapter, Krishna says that wherever the restless mind wanders, bring it back. A bead is a small, physical way to do that. The mind drifts to a bill, a text message, a song. The thumb moves to the next bead. The bead is the coming back, made into something you can feel.
screen: `MALA: A GARLAND FOR COUNTING.` · `THE MERU: THE BEAD YOU DON'T CROSS.` · `GEMS STRUNG ON ONE THREAD.` · `EACH BEAD IS A COMING BACK.`

segments.voice: Hold a mala if you have one, or touch the thumb to each fingertip in turn, saying your mantra once with each touch, silently or in a whisper; Om will do, or a word from your own tradition. When the mind drifts, don't scold it; let the next touch be the coming back. At the end of a round, pause, turn around, and go back the other way.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, the tool in the hand: the mala, its meru, and each bead as a small return.
Your line: each bead a coming back. A round has an end, and the meru tells you when you've reached it. That's day one thousand thirteen.

1014.title: mantra sadhana (a 40-day japa discipline)
1014.hook: who gets to hand you a mantra? the tradition gives more than one answer, and keeps them all
1014.howItsDone: In some Hindu lineages a mantra is received privately from a guru at diksha, initiation; in others, such as the public chanting of the divine names, the mantra is open to anyone who wants to say it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mala in the hand: the meru you don't cross, and each bead a coming back.

Who gets to hand you a mantra? In one family, a grandfather leans close to a teenager's ear at a ceremony and whispers a line meant for that ear alone, never to be said aloud to friends. In a park across town, a group sits in a circle singing names of God loud enough for joggers to hear, and anyone who wants to sit down is welcome to join. Both are mantra. Both are japa, in a way. And both have scripture behind them.
screen: `A LINE WHISPERED INTO ONE EAR.` → `NAMES SUNG IN A PARK.` → `BOTH HAVE SCRIPTURE BEHIND THEM.`

segments.voice: Start with the whisper. In some lineages, a mantra is received from a guru at diksha, initiation. The teacher chooses it and gives it, and the student keeps it private. The idea is that a mantra given this way carries the teacher's blessing and the lineage's practice behind it; there, picking one off a website isn't the same thing at all. Now the park. In a short text called the Kali-Santarana Upanishad, the sage Narada asks the god Brahma how to get through the hard age the tradition calls the Kali Yuga. Brahma answers with a mantra made of the names Hare, Rama and Krishna. Narada asks the obvious follow-up: what are the rules? And Brahma says there are none. Say it, and that's enough. Some communities point to that line for their open, public chanting. Then there's Om. In the Katha Upanishad, Death himself teaches a boy named Nachiketa that the word all the Vedas point to, the word sought by those who live in discipline, is Om. And some mantras are drawn from the old texts, like Om namah shivaya, honoring Shiva, whose words namah shivaya appear in the Shri Rudram. So how does someone choose? The tradition's honest answer: it depends on the path. A devotee of Krishna, a devotee of Shiva, a student of Vedanta and a beginner with no teacher may each be guided differently. What the answers share is that the mantra comes from somewhere; it isn't invented on the spot. And whichever is chosen, the sadhana is to stay with it.

1015.title: mantra sadhana (a 40-day japa discipline)
1015.hook: dawn and dusk are the hinges of the day; an old law book hangs the mantra on both
1015.howItsDone: Some Hindu families keep sandhya, a rite at dawn and dusk built around the Gayatri, and some who keep a mantra sadhana tie it to those same hinges of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, where the mantra comes from: a guru's diksha, the open names, the word the Vedas point to.

Just before sunrise, the street is gray. No color yet, no shadows. A man stands on a rooftop facing east, lips moving, and he doesn't sit down. He's waiting for something. Then the first edge of the sun clears the water tank on the next building, and he stops. That evening, on the same roof, he sits facing west and keeps going until the first star shows. He isn't watching a clock. He's watching the sky. It looks like a personal habit. It has a text behind it.
screen: `A ROOFTOP BEFORE SUNRISE.` → `STANDING UNTIL THE SUN SHOWS.` → `SITTING UNTIL THE FIRST STAR.`

segments.voice: The text is the Manusmriti, the Laws of Manu, one of the old books of dharma, in its second chapter. In paraphrase: at the morning twilight, one should stand, repeating the Savitri, the verse also known as the Gayatri, until the sun is seen. At the evening twilight, one should sit, repeating it until the stars appear. Notice there's no hour in it. The sky sets the edges: the sun's first appearance in the morning, the stars at night. The practice fills the in-between. The word for these joints of the day is sandhya, a joining, where night meets day and day meets night. The daily rite kept at those times is called sandhya too, and in some families it's still kept at dawn and dusk, with this verse at its heart. You don't need that rite to see what the timing gives a sadhana. A mantra hung on a hinge of the day doesn't need a reminder. The light changes, and the mantra comes with it. That's what the last week has been building. Pranayama sequences gave the breath an order and the stillness after. Then mantra sadhana: Krishna's answer to the restless mind, practice; a sankalpa to set the terms; the mala, each bead a coming back; and where the mantra comes from. Today adds the when. Not when it's convenient: when the day turns, morning or evening, whichever you can keep. A practice tied to a hinge, some teachers say, is easier to keep than one waiting for a free moment, because free moments rarely arrive on their own.
screen: `STAND AT DAWN UNTIL THE SUN SHOWS.` · `SIT AT DUSK UNTIL THE STARS APPEAR.` · `SANDHYA: THE JOINING OF THE DAY.` · `HANG THE MANTRA ON A HINGE.`

As it runs, choose your hinge, the first light or the last, the place where the mantra will start tomorrow, when the light changes and not when a free moment turns up.
